:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int 2x e^{x^2}\,\textrm d x.$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then both $u$ and its derivative $u'=2x$ appear in the integrand:

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} e^{\overbrace{x^2}^u}\,\textrm d x
$$

Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

Let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We now substitute our expressions into the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{2}}\,{{2x\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{\text{d}u} \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's evaluate the following definite integral:

$$
\displaystyle{\int_{0}^{3} xe^{x^{2}}\, \textrm{d}x}
$$

We'll use the change of variable method, which comprises three steps:

**Step1: ** Change of variable in the integrand.

Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = 2x 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u = x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

**Step 2:** Find the new limits of integration.

We create a table below to change our limits of integration from $x$ to $u{:}$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $9$ |

**Step 3:** Evaluate the integral in the new variable $u.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{9}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{9}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Often, there are several ways in which we can evaluate an integral using a change of variable. Whatever we use depends on the particular form of the integrand. In this tutorial, we take care of the applications of the properties
\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right) = e^x \quad \textrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(a^x\right) = a^x\ln a\]
which generally leads to nice integrands after the change of variable.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt {\ln 4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\ln 4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =4(\frac{15}{16}) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
